item.title: Receptor Abundance Alone Underpredicts Red Blood Cell Adhesion in Gaucher Disease
item.description: arXiv:2611.27960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Red blood cells (RBCs) in Gaucher disease (GD) adhere abnormally to vessel walls and carry more Lutheran/basal cell adhesion molecule (Lu/BCAM), a laminin receptor. Whether receptor abundance sets this adhesion is untested. We simulated RBCs carrying stochastic Lu/BCAM-laminin bonds, calibrated a population on control donors, and predicted GD adhesion from the 1.3-fold receptor rise. On laminin and endothelium the data exceed the prediction 1.6- to 1.7-fold. Matching them requires 2.4- and 4.6-fold more binding-competent receptors, compatible with the estimated 5.7-fold rise in phosphorylated receptors. Neither a stiffer membrane nor higher bond affinity removes the shortfall at high shear stress. In sickle cell disease, given active-receptor counts, the model predicts the fall in adhesion under hydroxyurea within 1.4-fold, while total receptors rise. Adhesion likely follows receptor state more than abundance. Stiffening instead retains cells at a splenic slit.
item.dc:creator: Zhaojie Chai, Pierre A. Buffet, Melanie Franco, George Em Karniadakis

item.title: E2Former-V3: Atom-Role-Aware Equivariant Interatomic Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.27111v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials approach density-functional accuracy, but explicit-solvent atom counts are dominated by hydrogens and water. Uniform equivariant architectures still give every atom the same latent width and number of expensive block updates. To our knowledge, no prior method reallocates capacity by chemical role while retaining every atom and its first-principles force. We introduce E2Former-V3, which treats capacity as an atom-level resource: a static chemical role, assigned before the backbone runs, sets each atom's latent width and update count. No atom is removed, no coordinate is integrated out, and every force remains the gradient of one conservative energy. Standard reduces only the update count, sending hydrogen through half as many full-width block updates; on OMol25 validation it reaches a force mean absolute error (MAE) of 8.146 meV/Angstrom, against E2Former-V2's published 8.38, at 1.75-1.84x V2's throughput with lower peak memory on one H200. Flash also narrows the low-resolution stream to one eighth of the high-resolution width (32 vs 256 channels) and routes water oxygen with hydrogen, reaching 4.00-4.88x on three solvated systems (up to 5.85x in the pure-water all-low-resolution limit) at 11.272 meV/Angstrom, trading force accuracy for speed. Across 54 20 ps MD legs, a 100 ps NVE check, and a 1 ns NVT run on a 32,437-atom solvated protein, all runs complete; the MD legs show no non-finite values, clashes, or water fusion, and water O-O and Na-O RDF peak positions match experiment within 0.04 Angstrom. E2Former-V3 therefore moves the accuracy-throughput frontier for all-atom, conservative simulation, not a uniform accuracy win: Standard is worse on biomolecules and metals, better on electrolytes and organics; energy MAE is higher than E2Former-V2's; and water densities remain about 7.5% too high. Code: https://github.com/IQuestLab/UBio-MolFM.
item.dc:creator: Frank Peng, Lin Huang, Arthur Jiang, Jia Zhang

item.title: Nutrient limitation drives Turing instabilities in cross-feeding microbial communities
item.description: arXiv:2611.27534v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Microbial communities are shaped by metabolic interactions, often in the form of cross-feeding in which microbes exchange metabolites via diffusion through the environment. We show here that the diffusion of cross-fed metabolites generically leads to a Turing instability in resource-poor environments, driven by the feedback between local metabolite availability and cell growth. A coarse-grained model of community biomass identifies the few dimensionless parameters that control the instability, most notably the ratio of environmental energy supply to cellular maintenance costs. We find that the detailed topology of the metabolic interaction network can be coarse-grained into a single effective parameter to quantitatively characterise the instability. Beyond the onset of the instability, the community forms compact aggregates whose merger is prevented by a competition for shared resources. Overall, our results demonstrate how spatial structure can arise as an inevitable consequence of metabolic interactions in a microbial community.
item.dc:creator: Jan Kocka, Steven A. Redford, Jaime Agudo-Canalejo, Kabir Husain

item.title: Biophysics of the Pyrenoid
item.description: arXiv:2607.05154v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Phase-separated liquid droplets organize molecules in cells, but the underlying physical principles differ from abiotic mixing and quantitative rules in living systems remain poorly understood. The pyrenoid -- a liquid-like organelle that enhances photosynthetic carbon fixation in algae and hornworts -- provides an unusually tractable model system. Here, we review recent advances in our understanding of pyrenoids from the perspective of biophysics. We highlight how reaction-diffusion models connect compartment architecture to catalytic performance, how soft matter theories link molecular interactions to condensate assembly, and how modern experimental methods enable these predictions to be tested quantitatively. Recent studies suggest that pyrenoid function may be described by a small number of effective transport and reaction processes, while condensate assembly can be understood through molecular design parameters and thermodynamic constraints. Together, these findings establish the pyrenoid as a powerful system for investigating catalytic compartmentalization, biomolecular self-organization and the emergence of effective physical descriptions in living systems.
item.dc:creator: Charley Schaefer, Mark Leake

item.title: Passive Entropy Rate Bounds the Information Required for Feedback Control
item.description: arXiv:2607.16639v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Living organisms across scales, along with many engineered devices, must control noisy systems with limited information to maintain a desired steady state. Here we ask how the performance of a feedback controller is limited by the rate at which information flows from sensors to control actions. We demonstrate that the minimum information rate required is the rate at which the passive dynamics increase the system's entropy. This general result allows us to quantify the information required to achieve a given target performance for a wide-ranging set of control problems. Next, we ask what explicit control protocol maximizes performance for a given information rate. We demonstrate that in many cases the best control strategy is to probabilistically time-reverse the uncontrolled passive dynamics. Implementing this protocol approaches or saturates our bound across a wide range of applications. We showcase these results through applications to stochastic bit control, nonlinear particle localization, microbial navigation, and experimentally realized information engines. Our findings pave the way for the study of feedback control in any settings where limited information is a key constraint, suggest principled explanations for microbial behavior, and provide new insights into fundamental questions regarding the thermodynamic value of information.
item.dc:creator: Matthew P. Leighton, Jose M. Betancourt, Thierry Emonet, Benjamin B. Machta, Michael C. Abbott
